Learning Objectives
Review the manner in which the treatment of polytrauma patients may differ from the
treatment of patients with an isolated orthopaedic injury.
Discuss the role of damage control orthopaedics and early appropriate care in the overall
treatment of polytrauma patients, including the coordination of care with other services.
Describe how injuries to the head/neck, chest, abdominopelvic viscera, and spine affect the
management of musculoskeletal injuries to the pelvis and extremities.
Review techniques for damage control orthopaedics and early appropriate care.

Trauma is a leading cause of morbidity and mortality among patients younger than 45 years,
with sequelae of musculoskeletal injury being a major contributor to long-term disability.
The timing and extent of surgical management can magnify or lessen the local and systemic
effects of trauma.
Damage control orthopaedics (DCO) is the provisional management of acute musculoskeletal
injuries to limit the physiologic effects of surgical treatment on a severely injured patient.
Early appropriate care (EAC) is the definitive management of the most critical fractures and
injuries after resuscitation, typically within 24 to 48 hours.

Introduction
In the United States, trauma is the leading cause of death and disability in individuals
younger than 45 years, accounting for 200,000 deaths each year and annual medical
expenses totaling more than $400 billion. Most deaths are associated with head injuries
or exsanguination immediately postinjury. Trauma care has evolved to reduce later
mortality and to mitigate other complications by treating patients based on their
physiology. In patients with adequate physiologic reserve, EAC is undertaken to
definitively manage musculoskeletal injuries early to allow for patient mobilization. In
severely injured patients without physiologic reserve, the expedited provisional
management of musculoskeletal injuries, known as DCO, decreases morbidity and
mortality.1 Expeditious and iterative patient assessment determines the response to
resuscitation so optimal musculoskeletal management, including the type and timing of
fracture management, may be undertaken.
In the 1980s, the advantages of early surgical fracture fixation were described, with an
emphasis on femoral shaft fractures.2 The concept of early total care led many providers
to address all extremity fractures during the same initial surgical setting. Early total care
was then questioned because more pulmonary complications and mortality were
reported in severely injured patients who underwent intramedullary nailing of the femur
within 24 hours postinjury.3,4
DCO was proposed as an alternative to early definitive fixation of femoral shaft fractures
in patients too severely injured to tolerate early definitive surgical treatment. In its

original conception, DCO was performed within hours postinjury, with a goal of less than
1 hour of surgical management. In the DCO algorithm, external fixation of femoral shaft
fractures quickly affords provisional skeletal stability and pain relief, facilitating nursing
care and upright posture while eliminating the need for skeletal traction with limited
blood loss and dissection. This strategy limits the physiologic effects of surgical
management. The DCO concept is used in patients who lack the physiologic reserve to
tolerate early definitive musculoskeletal surgery. DCO facilitates ongoing resuscitation
while limiting adverse effects locally and systemically by controlling hemorrhage,
facilitating patient positioning, and controlling the inflammatory effects of injury5
(Resource 1).
The EAC model6,7 involves determining the amount of surgical treatment a patient can
withstand. The emphasis is on early resuscitation with definitive fixation of the most
substantial injuries, such as femoral shaft and pelvis fractures, typically within 36 hours
postinjury. Determination of whether a patient is best suited for DCO versus EAC is best
achieved via collaborative decision making between the orthopaedic surgery, general
surgery trauma/acute care surgery, and anesthesia teams.
In developing a treatment plan for patients with multi-system injuries and unstable
fractures, an important consideration is whether a patient’s physiologic state has been
optimized to tolerate surgical treatment. The injury itself is considered the first hit to the
patient’s system and inflammatory cascade. Surgical management to stabilize fractures
affords control of bony bleeding, pain relief, and pulmonary benefits; however, surgical
management also may cause additional hemorrhage, fluid shifts, and hypothermia and
contribute to a secondary activation of the inflammatory cascade—the second hit.
Fracture fixation contributes to this response and may result in systemic inflammatory
response syndrome in under-resuscitated patients, depending on the amount of blood
loss, hypotension, or hypothermia generated via surgical management.8 Adequate
resuscitation is crucial in minimizing the effect of the second hit and its adverse
consequences. If the second hit exceeds a threshold level, severe systemic inflammation
may occur. In this model, systemic inflammatory response syndrome, which has been
associated with multi-organ failure and death, develops in severely injured patients.

Damage Control Orthopaedics
DCO is a treatment strategy focused on reducing the physiologic stress of early postinjury
surgical treatment in severely injured patients.
Patients in extremis or who have a borderline physiologic state are candidates for DCO.

Damage Control Orthopaedics
The goal of DCO is providing early, provisional wound management and fracture
stabilization while minimizing the effect, or second hit, of more extensive surgical
procedures. The second hit occurs if early surgical management results in additional
augmentation of the inflammatory response, promoting systemic inflammatory
response syndrome, acute respiratory distress syndrome, or even death.9 This
phenomenon can be avoided via resuscitation and the judicious use of DCO strategies
that reduce instability, hemorrhage, and inflammation.10
The DCO treatment strategy avoids longer definitive procedures associated with greater
blood loss and fluid shifts that increase the risk of hypothermia and coagulopathy and
exacerbate metabolic acidosis. Provisional fracture stabilization strategies used in DCO
may include circumferential pelvic antishock sheeting, skeletal traction, percutaneous
fracture reduction and fixation, and external fixation. Most long bone fractures and
many periarticular fractures and fracture-dislocations can be rapidly and effectively
stabilized via spanning external fixation.
The orthopaedic surgeon, trauma critical care team, and anesthesiologist must work
together to determine the appropriate timing of provisional and definitive fixation. This
timing typically is based on a patient’s resuscitation status and other factors known to
contribute to systemic coagulopathy, hypothermia, acute respiratory distress syndrome,
systemic inflammatory response syndrome, and higher mortality rates.11
Although no absolute criteria are available to determine which patients should be
treated via DCO, patients who require massive transfusion (>4 units of packed red blood
cells), patients with lactic acidosis, and patients with severe lung and/or head injuries are

candidates for DCO. Resuscitation may be ongoing in the operating room; however,
ongoing blood loss and progressive hypothermia often are associated with the operating
room/surgical setting, often making the intensive care unit (ICU) a better setting for
resuscitation after early, rapid DCO stabilization and hemorrhage control. The timing of
safe, definitive management of musculoskeletal injuries after DCO intervention typically
is based on the pace of resuscitation, normalization of vital signs, resolution of acidosis,
stabilization of fluid shifts, improvements in ventilation, and steady improvements in
neurologic and cardiopulmonary physiology.
Early Appropriate Care
EAC and definitive stabilization of musculoskeletal injuries in more stable patients leads to
earlier return to activity, with improved functional outcomes; shorter ICU and hospital stays;
and reduced incidence of complications, such as venous thromboembolism, nosocomial
pneumonia, and hospital-acquired pressure ulcers.
In resuscitated patients, this may include definitive fixation of any long bone fracture,
particularly the femur, and pelvic fractures within the first 36 hours, given that the patient
remains resuscitated and stable intraoperatively with a surgical team that is familiar with these
procedures.

Early Appropriate Care
In resuscitated patients, EAC is associated with low rates of pulmonary complications,
and hospital and ICU stays are minimized. Many studies have documented the
advantages of early stabilization in reducing morbidity and mortality, limiting the risk of
fat embolism, pneumonia, deep vein thrombosis, and sepsis, among other
complications.12-15 Early definitive long bone fixation is considered an integral aspect of
initial management; however, if a multiply injured patient requires surgical stabilization
of musculoskeletal injuries that necessitate prolonged surgical management or are
associated with major blood loss and transfusion, adequate resuscitation is critical
preoperatively.

EAC is considered in polytrauma patients who are normotensive and normothermic.
Priority is given to the management of long bone fractures, especially the femur;
dislocations; pelvic fractures; femoral neck fractures in young patients; and definitive
débridement of open injuries. Other fractures can be fixed as time allows. At any point, if
the patient’s condition deteriorates, DCO may need to be reinstituted.
Management Based on Physiologic and Laboratory Assessment
Vital signs and laboratory parameters are used to estimate postinjury blood loss and define
the degree of hemorrhagic shock and metabolic derangement.
pH, base excess/deficit, and serum lactate levels help define a patient’s resuscitation status,
with the following targets: pH level greater or equal to 7.25, base excess level less than or
equal to −5.5 mmol/L, and lactate level less than or equal to 4.0 mmol/L.
The degree of metabolic derangement and response to resuscitation are important in
determining if a patient is a candidate for EAC or requires DCO.

Management Based on Physiologic and Laboratory Assessment
Identification and characterization of shock are based on factors that include heart rate,
blood pressure, temperature, respiratory rate, urine output, and mental status.
Laboratory parameters routinely obtained during the treatment of multiply injured
patients include complete blood cell count, electrolyte level, international normalized
ratio, venous lactate level, and arterial blood gas level with pH and base excess/deficit
levels. Combined with physiologic parameters and physical examination findings, these
factors will guide resuscitation. Vital signs alone, especially in the younger, more fit
population, may mask ongoing hemorrhage until the patient becomes critically ill.
In patients with class I or class II hemorrhagic shock, intravenous access is established,
and 2 L of crystalloid is administered.16 Patients with greater or ongoing hemorrhage
require transfusions. To assess the response to resuscitation, vital signs are measured
continuously, and laboratory tests are repeated every 4 to 8 hours until they improve.
Critically ill patients with class IV hemorrhagic shock warrant initiation of a massive

transfusion protocol. Providing resuscitation with the use of fluid and blood products
restores tissue oxygenation, normalizing acidosis. Coagulopathy also is present in
patients who sustain massive hemorrhage postinjury. Massive resuscitation without
specific attention to clotting factors and platelets may accentuate coagulopathy via
dilution. Transfusion ratios for platelets and fresh frozen plasma have been proposed,
with initial studies supporting 1:1:1 administration of packed red blood cells, platelets,
and fresh frozen plasma in severe cases.17
Severe musculoskeletal trauma and its associated hemorrhage results in tissue
hypoperfusion, which leads to acidosis. Normalization of these values within 24 hours
postinjury is predictive of survival18 (Resource 2). Lactate level is considered the most
reliable indicator of resuscitation because pH and base excess levels are less specific and
subject to confounders, such as alcohol ingestion and renal disease. Parameters for the
adequacy of resuscitation include improving acidosis, as measured by a pH level of 7.25
or higher, a base excess level of −5.5 mmol/L or higher, or a lactate level of less than 4.0
mmol/L. Definitive fracture management (EAC) may be performed if a severe head injury
or other medical pathology does not preclude such treatment.19
EAC typically involves surgical stabilization of all spinal, pelvic, acetabular, and femoral
fractures within 24 to 48 hours postinjury. If one or more of the aforementioned
laboratory parameters are unlikely to be met within this time frame, DCO is performed
to facilitate resuscitation. The clinical picture and vital signs also are used to determine
the timing and type of management (EAC or DCO). DCO indicates that the patient should
undergo rapid provisional soft-tissue débridement and provisional fracture stabilization,
thereby limiting surgical time and blood loss to minimize the progression of metabolic
derangement (ie, acidosis and coagulopathy)20 (Figure 1; Resource 3).

Prioritization of Systemic and Musculoskeletal Injuries
Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS) protocol is the standard of care by which injured
patients are evaluated on presentation.
Primary, secondary, and tertiary surveys are required elements of the ATLS protocol,
facilitating systematic identification of injuries and avoiding missed injuries.
Rapid identification of injuries during the primary and/or secondary survey help to determine
if a patient requires DCO or EAC.

Prioritization of Systemic and Musculoskeletal Injuries
Selection of the type and timing of treatment for a patient with multi-system trauma
should be undertaken in a collaborative fashion, including all members of the

multidisciplinary trauma team. In trauma patients, injuries should be identified via
implementation of ATLS protocol.
The American College of Surgeons Committee on Trauma developed ATLS algorithms for
the initial evaluation and treatment of trauma victims. The primary survey identifies the
location and severity of most injuries and determines the patient’s physiologic status,
including the presence of shock. Hypovolemic shock is most frequently encountered
after trauma, especially in patients with a pelvic ring injury, long bone fracture, and/or
multiple open fractures. Shock results in tissue hypoperfusion, hypoxemia, activation of
the inflammatory cascade, and immune dysfunction. Reduction and fixation of fractures
helps control hemorrhage, aiding in resuscitation.
During the ATLS primary survey, life- and limb-threatening injuries, including massive
hemorrhage from a pelvic fracture or multiple long bone fractures, neurovascular injury
resulting in ischemia or neurologic dysfunction of an extremity, and compartment
syndrome should be identified. These types of injuries must be addressed emergently—
within minutes to hours. In these situations, orthopaedic management, specifically DCO,
substantially contributes to resuscitation, promotes survival of the patient, and
preserves limb function.
During the ATLS secondary survey, the remaining musculoskeletal injuries are identified.
Many of these acute injuries ideally are managed on an urgent basis—within hours to
days—given that the patient has been adequately resuscitated. These injuries include
open fractures; fractures associated with considerable soft-tissue injury (fracture
blisters, Morel-Lavallee lesions); and mechanically unstable injuries of the spine, pelvis,
and acetabulum and proximal and diaphyseal femur fractures; such injuries benefit from
provisional or definitive stabilization within 36 hours. Most other acute fractures are
appropriately managed within 7 to 14 days postinjury. EAC permits rapid mobilization in
appropriately resuscitated patients.
ATLS tertiary surveys are crucial to avoid injuries that may have been missed during the
primary or secondary surveys. Optimally, these examinations typically are performed if
the patient can be interactive and express symptoms or show signs of injury that may be
less obvious to the examining provider. Performance of at least one, if not multiple,

tertiary examinations is critical to avoid missed injuries that may lead to additional

Fracture Management
Acute fracture management, following the principles of DCO or EAC, plays a critical role in pain
management, hemorrhage control, and mechanical stabilization of bone and soft tissues in
polytrauma patients.
The ability of an orthopaedic surgeon to rapidly stabilize fractures has a considerable effect on
the overall morbidity and mortality associated with polytrauma.

Fracture Management
The essential goals of orthopaedic management include resuscitation, pain relief,
improved fracture alignment and stability, and enhanced mobility to ultimately restore
optimal function. Pain from musculoskeletal injury also induces sympathetic discharge,
which may contribute to a hyperinflammatory response, increasing the risks of
morbidity and mortality. Similarly, uncontrolled pain contributes to continued immobility
and thromboembolic events, pulmonary complications, and death.21 Fracture
stabilization reduces pain and narcotic use, potentially resulting in milder respiratory
depression and fewer instances of other adverse effects.
Early reduction and fixation of fractures is important in the resuscitation and pain relief
of trauma patients. Unstable long bone fractures often are managed definitively within
the first 24 hours postinjury. Periarticular fractures benefit from early reduction but may
require delayed definitive management because of soft-tissue compromise. Poorly timed
or poorly executed surgical management is associated with a risk of wound healing and
infection. Provisional external fixation frequently is performed within 48 hours to control
alignment and afford acute pain relief, with definitive internal fixation performed days or
weeks postinjury. After long bone, pelvic, and periarticular fractures are stabilized,
mobility improves, facilitating an upright posture, which enhances ventilation and

decreases the risks of pulmonary and thromboembolic complications and pressure
ulceration of the skin.
Associated Soft-Tissue Injury
Soft-tissue injuries associated with fractures, such as open fractures; Morel-Lavallee lesions;
extensive abrasions; nerve and blood vessel injury; and compartment syndrome influence the
fracture management strategy.
Soft-tissue injuries may increase the risk of infection, nonunion, and poor functional
outcomes.
Early recognition and management may limit these adverse effects.

Associated Soft-Tissue Injury
Many high-energy injuries are associated with severe soft-tissue damage. Soft-tissue
injuries include but are not limited to lacerations, abrasions, blisters, open and closed
degloving injuries (ie, Morel-Lavallee lesions), crush injuries, and compartment
syndrome. Compartment syndrome must be managed emergently to avoid the
complications of nerve dysfunction, rhabdomyolysis, and myonecrosis. Open fractures,
contaminated wounds/lacerations, and degloving wounds (open or closed) typically are
managed urgently (within 12 to 24 hours) to minimize the risk of infection and
progressive tissue destruction.22 Fractures associated with blisters, swelling below the
threshold of compartment syndrome, and superficial abrasions may be managed acutely
with a higher risk of infection and wound complications. Alternatively, these injuries
often are managed in a delayed fashion via initial provisional reduction/fixation to allow
for soft-tissue stabilization and later conversion to definitive fixation after the soft
tissues are amenable to additional surgical management. This staged protocol aims to
minimize wound healing problems and infection.
Soft-tissue management is integrated in DCO and EAC. The surgeon must identify a
patient’s eligibility for EAC versus DCO. A clear understanding of the manner in which
various treatment options for bone and soft-tissue injuries affect the timing, blood loss,

and overall physiologic stress on a patient is critical to determining whether EAC versus

Orthopaedic Treatment of Polytrauma Patients
Initial Management
As orthopaedic injuries are recognized during evaluation, they are managed to limit ongoing
injury caused by unstable fractures and dislocations.
Deformed limbs are restored to more anatomic positions, occasionally without radiographs,
restoring perfusion and relieving pressure on articular surfaces, nerves, and skin.
Wounds are assessed for tissues involved and the degree of contamination.
Hemorrhage is controlled with the use of pressure dressings and a tourniquet if necessary.
Techniques
Closed reduction and splint immobilization of fractures
Closed reduction and splint immobilization of fractures is critical for establishing initial
alignment, stability, and pain control for all patients, including those undergoing DCO or EAC.
Initial reduction and splint immobilization are especially important in patients undergoing
DCO because many injuries, particularly those that are closed and more peripheral, are likely
to be managed in a delayed fashion.
The stability afforded via splint immobilization facilitates transport and enhances patient
positioning for enhanced ventilation and decubitus prophylaxis.
Splint immobilization often is preferred over cast immobilization because it helps
accommodate swelling, is easier to remove, and provides limited ability to assess the
underlying tissues without removal.
Skeletal traction
Skeletal traction is a mode of provisional stabilization and reduction that can be applied
rapidly, safely, percutaneously, and with limited stress to the patient or blood loss.
It should replace femoral fracture transportation traction devices, such as Hare or Thomas
splints, which may compress neurovascular structures and promote compartment
syndrome.

Although skeletal traction may be used during DCO or EAC, it may be the only feasible mode
of provisional stabilization for a patient in extremis in certain DCO scenarios.
Skeletal traction is commonly used to manage injuries of the pelvis, acetabulum, and the
proximal lower extremity.
It may involve the use of tensioned wire or a transfixion pin placed within the distal femur,
proximal tibia, distal tibia, or calcaneus (Figure 2).
Skeletal traction functions via ligamentotaxis.
Occasionally, if the deformity is caused by bone herniating through the fascia, traction will
not be successful, and an alternative reduction strategy must be used.

reduces contamination and restores skeletal alignment and stability, with the goal of
minimizing hypothermia, hypovolemia/anemia, hypotension, metabolic derangement, and
shock

External fixation
Early fixation is an essential aspect of fracture management in patients requiring DCO.23
Simple external fixation devices can be applied in the emergency department or ICU, if
necessary, to achieve reduction and stabilization.
However, some studies have shown that traction may afford adequate temporary femur
stabilization in polytrauma patients.24
If performed in the operating room, more sophisticated constructs can be used to facilitate
stabilization (Figures 3 and 4).
External fixation devices may be used for the management of closed or open fractures and
fractures of the upper extremity, lower extremity, and pelvis.
Uniplanar external fixation, such as a four-pin frame for a long bone fracture or a joint
spanning frame, can be rapidly applied.
DCO with external fixation of femoral shaft fractures is appropriate in patients too unstable
to tolerate definitive surgical treatment within 24 to 36 hours.
Provisional external fixation is safely converted to internal fixation as long as 2 to 3 weeks
postinjury before the risk of infection considerably increases.
Joint spanning frames are useful in the staged management of periarticular fractures
associated with severe swelling to avoid wound complications and infection.

Fasciotomies
Fasciotomies are indicated in patients in whom compartment syndrome has been diagnosed
via clinical signs/symptoms or compartment pressure monitoring before permanent muscle
and nerve injury occurs at 6 to 8 hours.
Compartment syndrome is commonly associated with high-energy trauma to the lower leg
but may occur in any area in which tissue compartments exist.

Compartment syndrome occurs in patients with open or closed fractures and even in
patients without a fracture.
A fasciotomy consists of incising the fascial envelope to relieve interstitial tissue pressure and
restore perfusion of the compartment (Figure 5).
Although technically not compartment syndrome, areas in which neurovascular structures
are highly constrained, such as the carpal tunnel, also may require concomitant release.
Prophylactic fasciotomies are indicated if a body part has experienced ischemia for
approximately 4 to 6 hours and revascularization, via reduction, pressure relief, or vascular
repair, has been achieved.
During reperfusion, swelling occurs, leading to delayed compartment syndrome, which can
be avoided via early fasciotomy.

management of compartment syndrome. Spanning external fixation was used to manage the
associated tibial plateau fracture. (Courtesy of Andrew R. Evans, MD, FACS, FAAOS, Providence,
RI.)
Percutaneous provision stabilization of fractures
Percutaneous provisional stabilization of fractures and dislocations may be beneficial in DCO
scenarios in which rapid control of fracture fragments is required to prevent progressive
neurovascular injury or to offload overlying soft tissues.
Percutaneous stabilization for highly unstable fracture patterns often is not definitive but
must achieve desired goals.

A prominent tibial tubercle avulsion fragment in patients with a proximal tibia fracture is an
example of an injury that would benefit from provisional percutaneous reduction and screw
fixation, with or without spanning external fixation and subsequent definitive staged
management.
In skilled hands, certain fractures may be amenable to subcutaneous or submuscular
bridging plate fixation in a DCO setting.
Limited débridement of open wounds
In the DCO setting, the ideal débridement may not be possible, especially in patients with
complex or highly contaminated wounds.
However, more limited débridement in the emergency department or the operating room
will minimize the burden of contamination and necrotic tissue.
In DCO, gross contamination and clearly necrotic tissue is excised to limit the risk of infection
and the burden of toxic metabolites. The extent of such débridement and the time taken to
achieve optimal débridement are limited by the patient’s response to resuscitation, possibly
necessitating early repeat débridement as the patient’s condition improves. Such a strategy
may avoid premature débridement of tissues in a transition zone between necrotic and
viable tissue.
Radical excisional débridement and/or immediate amputation may be required in patients
with a severe open injury or in patients in extremis.
Although open fractures ideally should be managed within several hours postinjury to
minimize bacterial adherence and glycocalyx production, recent studies demonstrate
acceptable rates of infection in patients who undergo surgical débridement of open fractures
within 12 to 24 hours.22,25-28
Open fractures and dislocations are managed urgently and should be given priority in
critically ill patients who are stable enough to tolerate short surgical procedures.
Amputation
Amputation may be required in patients with a severe open wound, fracture, or ischemic
limb and in patients in extremis.
Amputation may help rapidly achieve hemostasis if salvage or reconstruction may threaten
the patient’s life via hemorrhage or sepsis.
Ideally, a consensus among the treating surgical and anesthesia physicians helps justify
amputation clinically and medicolegally because the patient typically is unable to provide
consent.
Informative discussion with the patient's family preoperatively is recommended if possible.

Preperitoneal pelvic packing (PPP)
PPP is a strategy for treating hemodynamically unstable patients with a pelvic ring injury and
who are in hemorrhagic shock.29
PPP is considered an effective treatment option to control pelvic hemorrhage if integrated
into a multidisciplinary approach that includes resuscitation, pelvic reduction/stabilization,
and angioembolization.
PPP typically is performed in the same surgical setting as pelvic ring reduction and
stabilization to tamponade venous bleeding.
Sponge packs are applied via a Pfannenstiel incision along the periphery of the true pelvis to
tamponade bleeding structures.
Packs typically are left in place for 24 to 48 hours, with a planned return to the operating
room for pack removal, reexamination for bleeding sources, and definitive pelvic fixation,
depending on the patient’s physiologic status.
Arterial injuries typically require angioembolization or surgical ligation.
The current indications for PPP are based on clinical practice guidelines and require
additional research.30
Wound management
In a DCO setting, meticulous wound closure of complex wounds may not be possible.
Wound packing can help achieve hemostasis and prevent tissue desiccation.
Wound packing may be performed in the emergency department, operating room, or ICU.
Vacuum-assisted wound closure devices also are useful for wound management (Figure 6);
however, in DCO scenarios, negative pressure dressings necessitate caution because the
technique can exacerbate hemorrhage in patients with a large open wound and
coagulopathy.

Early Appropriate Care
A comprehensive care strategy that provides definitive management of musculoskeletal
injuries.
Techniques used in the management of isolated fractures prioritize the management of long
bones and pelvic fractures.
The goals of EAC are to achieve definitive hemostasis, comprehensive débridement, fracture
reduction with definitive stable fixation, and closure/containment of the soft-tissue envelope,
including primary amputation if necessary.
EAC is performed with a prioritized plan of action given that the patient is stabile after
resuscitation; however, if the patient shows signs of instability (refractory tachycardia,
hypotension, or coagulopathy) during EAC procedures, DCO strategies may need to be
initiated.
Techniques
Systematic excisional débridement of traumatic wounds
Systematic excisional débridement of traumatic wounds is required to remove necrotic
tissue and foreign debris that may predispose the wound to infection.

This typically can be achieved if the severely injured patient is sufficiently stable to undergo
EAC but may require considerable time in patients with a complex wound.
If a wound is to be closed after initial débridement, definitive and complete débridement of
any foreign or necrotic debris must be achieved.
During initial débridement, the surgeon must be acutely aware of tissues around the margin
of traumatic wounds that may represent a zone of evolving necrosis that may initially appear
viable but ultimately may succumb to necrosis over the following hours or days.
Soft tissue that is deemed questionable during initial débridement may be excisionally
débrided and later reconstructed rather than preserved and reevaluated in a timely fashion
to reduce the need for reconstruction or diminish the resultant disability.
In addition, elimination of foreign body contamination may be difficult to achieve in patients
with an open wound with extensive contamination. Such patients may require multiple
staged débridement procedures or radical débridement during the initial surgical setting to
avoid wound infection and sepsis.
External fixation
External fixation (uniplanar versus multiplanar) is a useful treatment option for the
provisional or definitive fixation of fractures.
External fixator design by itself does not define the DCO versus EAC treatment strategy.
If used in the EAC setting, indications for external fixation include staged management of
complex periarticular fractures or a fracture pattern and associated conditions that make
external fixation the optimal treatment modality.
External fixator designs include uniplanar and circular external fixators and internal fixators
(Figure 7) that are applied in the pelvis.31
Circular external fixator constructs with rods (commonly referred to as Ilizarov frames) and
an adjustable hexapod frame (Taylor spatial frame) may be useful for certain fractures with
associated soft-tissue constraints but typically are applied in a staged fashion and not during
EAC.

Plate/screw fixation
Plate and screw fixation of fractures typically is reserved for EAC scenarios because it often
involves more surgical time, blood loss, and surgical stress.
In addition to resuscitation status, the status of the overlying soft-tissue envelope, the
fracture complexity, and the fixation strategy (bridge plating versus anatomic compression
plating) help determine the fixation strategy (Figure 8).
Open reduction and internal fixation may be required, particularly for periarticular injuries,
requiring more extensive dissection with biologic disruption and surgical duration than
appropriate for EAC.
Soft-tissue conditions also may preclude open reduction and internal fixation during EAC.

Intramedullary nail fixation 
Intramedullary nail fixation also is a time-tested, highly reliable reduction and fixation
strategy for fractures of the lower and upper extremity. 
In patients who are well resuscitated, fractures of the femoral and tibial shaft are particularly
amenable to intramedullary nailing, resulting in very high rates of fracture union if used
according to the principles of biologic osteosynthesis. 
Caution should be exercised in patients with bilateral femur fractures, with some studies
reporting an increased rate of complications.32,33

Limb salvage versus amputation
Limb salvage versus amputation is a topic beyond the scope of this lesson.
Briefly, determination of whether a particular injury is amenable to limb salvage versus
amputation depends on numerous patient factors, surgeon factors, injury variables, and
hospital resources.
The determination often can be made after initial débridement, at which time the extent of
bony and soft-tissue injury is more fully appreciated.
The patient may be engaged in shared decision making at this time if the reconstruction
course and expected outcome can be projected.
Under the EAC model, initial extremity débridement and provisional fracture stabilization
may be the most appropriate course of action, with planned staged débridement procedures
or delayed amputation, depending on the situation.
In situations in which DCO is critical for a patient in extremis, amputation may be a primary
lifesaving measure.
In the most severe circumstances, limb salvage attempts can increase the risk of mortality.

Special Considerations: Concomitant Injuries
Head Injury

Head Injury
Concurrent head injuries are common in orthopaedic trauma patients. Continuing
hemorrhage or hypotension from the injury or surgical management will exacerbate the
head injury. Most head injuries are minor, with presenting Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS)
scores higher than 12. Post-resuscitation Glasgow Coma Scale scores correlate with
functional outcomes.34 Progressive deterioration of mental status develops in fewer
than 3% of patients with a mild head injury; therefore, CT of the head is performed
liberally in patients presenting with new trauma. Patients with severe head injury
(Glasgow Coma Scale score ≤8) are comatose, requiring mechanical ventilation and ICU
monitoring.
The timing of fracture fixation in patients with a severe head injury has been a long-
standing topic of debate. Most studies have focused on femoral shaft fractures and
support a strategy of DCO in patients with elevated an intracranial pressure and limited
cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP).19 CPP is calculated as the mean arterial pressure
minus the intracranial pressure. A CPP less than 70 mm Hg reduces brain perfusion and
may cause permanent damage. To proceed with definitive fixation, intracranial pressure
should be less than or equal to 20 mm Hg and CPP should be greater or equal to 70 mm
Hg, and fracture surgical management should not be associated with hemorrhage or
hypotension.35 DCO via external fixation of femur and pelvis fractures is appropriate.36
In polytrauma patients with a blunt traumatic brain injury, the need for blood
replacement and intraoperative hypovolemia substantially increases the risk of inpatient
neurologic rehabilitation, the cost of disability, and the risk of mortality.37

Chest injuries, including pulmonary contusion, pneumothorax, hemothorax, blunt
cardiac injury, and traumatic aortic aneurysm, also are common in trauma patients. Even
minor chest injuries are problematic because they increase the risk of pulmonary
complications. Chest injuries are painful and cause splinting. Poor inspiratory effort is
further promoted via narcotic medications that suppress the respiratory drive, and
recumbency contributes to poor ventilation, accentuating the risk of adverse sequelae.
Direct parenchymal lung damage in patients with pulmonary contusions and other
severe chest trauma further diminishes oxygenation. The posttraumatic inflammatory
response may exacerbate the pulmonary injury, resulting in acute respiratory distress
syndrome.
Fracture reduction and stabilization promotes pain relief, upright posture, and mobility
from bed, all of which reduce the risks of pulmonary and other complications.
Historically, the early definitive management of femoral and other fractures in poorly
resuscitated patients with severe chest/pulmonary injury was associated with higher
risks of pulmonary complications (acute respiratory distress syndrome, systemic
inflammatory response syndrome) and mortality in some studies.38 More recent studies
have shown that although major chest injury is a risk factor for pulmonary
complications, the early definitive fixation of axial and femoral fractures in resuscitated
patients is associated with fewer complications than delayed surgical management, even
in patients with a severe chest injury.39 Otherwise, DCO is implemented via traction or
external fixation of femoral and pelvic fractures.

Abdominal Injury
Abdominal injuries from blunt or penetrating trauma, such as liver or splenic lacerations,
bowel perforations, mesenteric dissections/ischemia, and retroperitoneal injuries,
commonly occur in patients with multiple injuries, necessitating early advanced imaging
studies and potentially exploratory laparotomy. The increased availability of high-quality
diagnostic imaging studies (ie, focused assessment via sonography in trauma, CT pan-
scan, CT angiography) has facilitated the rapid and specific characterization of abdominal

common, reducing the number of patients who undergo laparotomy. Some of the most

musculoskeletal trauma. According to numerous studies, the highest morbidity and
mortality rates are reported in patients with these injury combinations.40-42
Multidisciplinary treatment in such patients requires algorithm-based care. Life-
threatening injuries are managed first. In patients with combined pelvic ring and
abdominal injuries, provisional reduction and external fixation of the pelvic ring injury
should be performed in patients with amenable fracture patterns before laparotomy.
This protocol provides better venous tamponade in the pelvis and prevents additional
enlargement of the pelvic diameter. In critically ill patients with persistent hemodynamic
instability and/or acidosis, DCO, including the use of a pelvic binder/sheet, should be
implemented in the initial setting.43
Vascular Injury

Vascular Injury
Vascular injury may be associated with injuries in any area, including the
pelvis/acetabulum and the upper and lower extremities. Arterial and/or venous injury
may precipitate hemorrhagic shock, requiring immediate attention during the primary
survey. Central arterial and venous injuries (aorta, vena cava, brachiocephalic, common
iliac) typically are managed by acute care surgeons, general surgeons, and vascular
surgeons via clamping with or without open surgical repair; percutaneous endovascular
stents; or emerging technologies/techniques, such as resuscitative endovascular balloon
occlusion of the aorta.44 Vascular injury with limb ischemia represents a threatened limb
and necessitates emergent restoration of perfusion within 6 hours to avoid critical
ischemia and amputation.
Rapid identification of a threatened limb is necessary to mobilize the resources to
potentially salvage the limb. Close communication between vascular surgery,

Spinal Column and/or Spinal Cord Injury

Spinal Column and/or Spinal Cord Injury
Spinal column injury is common in trauma patients. Spinal column injuries at any level
may be associated with neurologic injury, necessitating close evaluation. Unstable
injuries to the thoracolumbar spine and fractures of the pelvis or femur requiring bed
rest and recumbency until stabilized pose a constraint to patients. Therefore, an
increasing body of literature has reported fewer complications and shorter hospital
length of stays with fewer days of mechanical ventilation if these injuries are stabilized
early.45 The surgical stabilization of spinal column injuries is advocated within 24 to 48
hours in resuscitated patients. A spine damage control strategy also has been described,
in which the first of two stages of surgical management occur early, affording mechanical
stability, pain relief, and better posturing.46
Spinal cord injury with neurogenic shock may substantially contribute to a patient’s
overall hemodynamic stability profile and, therefore, play a considerable role in
determining if a DCO or EAC treatment strategy is required. The American Spinal Injury
Association Impairment Scale is used to classify spinal cord injuries. In patients with a
spinal cord injury, most surgeons advocate decompressive surgical management for the
neurologic elements. Surgical timing for spinal cord decompression remains
controversial. Decompression may involve reduction of fractures and dislocations
because the neural elements may be under pressure from bone, disk material,
hematoma, or foreign material. Incomplete injuries are decompressed in an emergent or
urgent manner because improvement in neurologic function is possible.

Extremity fracture care in patients with a spine injury is determined via coordination of
care between the spine and extremity surgeons, with input from the trauma critical care
team. Decision factors include the complexity of the injuries, patient positioning needs
for surgical treatment, and patient resuscitation status. In patients with a partial or
complete neurologic deficit, fracture reduction and fixation are necessary to facilitate
long-term nursing care and avoid ulceration. In paraplegic patients and quadriplegic
patients, optimal upper extremity function is critical for mobility and activities of daily
living.
Collaboration Strategies to Coordinate Care
Emergency Department
Trauma team activation protocol
American College of Surgeons verified level 1 trauma centers typically have a multi-tiered
trauma activation system that is defined at the state or institutional level.
Trauma activation criteria are based on the clinical needs of the injured patient and define
the following:
Which members of the multidisciplinary emergency response/trauma team need to be
present
When members of the multidisciplinary emergency response/trauma team need to be
present
How members of the multidisciplinary emergency response/trauma team are notified
Orthopaedic surgery plays a critical role in the multidisciplinary immediate evaluation and
management of polytrauma patients, especially those with threatened (ischemic) extremities
associated with fractures or dislocations, open injuries, pelvic injuries, and multiple fractures.
Acute care surgery/trauma surgery evaluates and coordinates timely surgical management,
support of resuscitation, and critical care services.
ATLS protocol defines how and when to include orthopaedics, ideally during the primary
survey because circulatory/hemorrhage control is critical to patient stabilization.
Communication is critical in achieving successful coordination of care among members of the
orthopaedic service and the network of trauma providers in the hospital.

Surgical subspecialty providers
Vascular surgery—Threatened limb management must be initiated in a timely fashion
because time is of the essence. The time of limb ischemia begins at the time of injury not at
the time of arrival at the hospital. Ischemic limbs need to be perfused within a maximum of
6 hours before irreversible necrosis occurs. Advocate for temporizing measures, such as
shunts, that facilitate rapid revascularization and the coordination of proper sequencing of
orthopaedic and vascular reconstructive components of procedures.
Cardiothoracic surgery: involve in cases of scapulothoracic dissociation and sternoclavicular
fracture/dislocations.
Urology: work collaboratively in cases involving pelvic injuries with bladder/urethral injuries;
coordination of care will help optimize surgical management strategies if cystograms
and/or bladder repairs are necessary, in the management of urogenital injuries, for
ureteral stenting, and in considering the manner in which and the timing of suprapubic
catheter implementation.
Gynecology—Vaginal, perineal, and rectal open pelvic injuries are critical to detect in a
timely fashion to avoid rapid development of intrapelvic abscesses and life-threatening
sepsis. Mortality rates are extremely high in patients with an open pelvic ring injury that is
missed for more than 24 to 48 hours. A standardized set of criteria for determining the
timing of speculum examination by emergency department and/or gynecology will help
prevent missed injuries.
Plastic surgery: notify early if wounds cannot be closed primarily and if soft-tissue
reconstruction is anticipated
Nursing/care coordination—Severe trauma is highly disruptive to the lives of trauma victims
and their families. Maintaining nursing awareness of orthopaedic care strategies will help to
facilitate and coordinate all aspects of patient care and greatly improve patient satisfaction.
Social workers and case managers play an integral role in facilitating care after acute
hospitalization and coordinating communication with families of trauma victims. Engaging
these resources as early in the patient’s hospital course as possible is critical in helping
patients navigate posttraumatic hospitalization and enables patients to exhibit greater self-
efficacy in managing and complying with their care.
